title: The hypertrophy series: full range of motion vs partials
summary: NH explains that full ROM is a tool rather than a rule, mostly about not cutting the negative. Full ROM gives the most tonnage and time under tension so it should make up most training, while scheduled partials like rack pulls and pin presses isolate specific regions. Skipping lockout on most lifts is fine except deadlifts.
claims: Full ROM lengthens the muscle longer and raises time under tension
Full ROM is subjective: a deadlift with smaller plates or from a hole has more range; you use ROM for its benefits, not as an obligation
Most ROM cutting is on the negative, chopping the hardest bottom portion to be stronger
Cutting the negative also cuts the positive, so too little stretch and contraction for hypertrophy
Not fully locking out on bench, overhead press or squat doesn't hurt gains and keeps tension on the muscle while protecting tendons
Deadlifts are the exception: soft lockouts usually mean thoracic rounding, so lock out fully
Full ROM yields the most tonnage, time under tension and lengthening, plus mobility
Training only short ranges leaves you weak where a slipping weight may push you, so you get hurt
Partials must be scheduled with intent, never improvised after failing a rep
Partials such as pin presses and rack pulls let you lift more weight and target muscles the full lift underuses
The deadlift's hardest part, getting past the knee, is posterior chain; a below-knee rack pull shifts emphasis to the upper back and traps
Partials isolate regions better while full ROM gives more total tonnage
Most training should be full ROM with a portion of partials; training only partials misses the point unless you're a specialist
